newsitem.title: POLAND: American Jewish Committee backs Polish NATO bid.
newsitem.headline: American Jewish Committee backs Polish NATO bid.

text.p: Officials of The American Jewish Committee (AJC) said on Tuesday their organisation backed Poland's drive to join NATO and this process should not be blocked by controversy over the restitution of Jewish property.

"The AJC and its board of governors, meeting in New York last week, passed a resolution supporting the expansion of NATO to include Poland," Marc Ittelson, AJC assistant director of European Affairs, told a news conference in Warsaw.

Leaders of the Israel-based World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO) have said they may lobby against Poland's admission unless Warsaw does more to restore Jewish property taken over by communist authorities after Nazi occupiers murdered most of Poland's Jews in World War Two.

As the WJRO is linked with the U.S.-based World Jewish Congress (WJC), Polish officials fear this stance might harm chances of securing the two-thirds of votes in the U.S. Senate needed in future to ratify Poland's admission to NATO.

The fact-finding delegation of the influential AJC, which has 32 offices in the United States, said such comments were not representative of all American Jewry and even if the WJRO opposed ratification the Committee would support it.

"There have been statements by some groups that have tried to couple...the issue of restitution and the issue of support for Poland's entrance into NATO," said Jeffrey Weintraub, director of the AJC-tied Center for American Pluralism.
"We have expressly pointed out that it is wrong to couple those two and we should take each separately," Weintraub said.
Poland expects to be invited at the Western defence pact's Madrid summit next week, along with Hungary and the Czech Republic, to start talks leading to NATO entry in 1999.
But its admission must be confirmed by legislatures of all 16 member states -- specifically by 67 of the 100 U.S. senators.
Last month Polish newspapers reported that WJRO leaders had vowed to block Polish, Czech and Romanian membership of NATO, saying they had not done enough to restore Jewish property.

Most of the 3.5 million Jews who lived in Poland before the war were killed by the Germans and others later left partly because of anti-Semitic episodes including a 1946 pogrom and and a campaign by part of the ruling communist party in 1968.
Representatives of the few thousand remaining Jews in Poland issued a statement last week supporting NATO entry.
Warsaw's democratic governments since the 1989 fall of communism have sought to improve relations with Jews worldwide.
Parliament this year passed a law paving the way for return of some communal property to Jewish congregations.
But Warsaw insists that when it passes a general law on return or compensation to all Poles for private property taken by the communists, only resident Polish citizens will qualify.
Some Jewish organisations abroad say a special case should be made for Holocaust survivors and their heirs now abroad, while Warsaw says all claimants should be treated alike.
The AJC representatives, in Poland on a fact-finding trip, said there were arguments for making a special case for Jews over private property but this required careful consideration.
